text: Chapter 3 covered scheduled analytics rules, which generate an alert automatically the moment their logic matches. This lesson covers a different tool: the hunting query, which an analyst runs manually, on demand, to look for activity that has never triggered an automated detection in the first place, and which plugs directly into the SOC maturity model the previous course taught.

A hunting query is a KQL query too, but it isn't scheduled and it doesn't generate an alert on its own. An analytics rule can only ever catch a pattern someone already thought to formalize into a rule. A hunting query lets an analyst go looking for a pattern nobody has written a rule for yet, which closes exactly the gap a purely reactive SOC can never close by sitting back and waiting for alerts alone.

Take the earlier course's own example: a slow data exfiltration that stays just under every correlation rule's threshold, so nothing ever fires. A hunting query built around a different question, which accounts have sustained low-volume outbound transfer over the past thirty days, can surface exactly that activity, because it isn't waiting for a threshold to trip. It's actively looking.

Sentinel ships a built-in hunting query gallery, a library of pre-built KQL organized by tactic like credential access and lateral movement, that Microsoft maintains and an analyst can run against their own workspace without writing KQL from scratch. Running gallery queries regularly is itself a genuinely proactive practice, but the gallery can't anticipate every environment's own specific risk, so a maturing hunting program also writes custom hunting queries targeted at patterns unique to that organization.

A hunt that finds something real doesn't stay a one-off finding. An analyst can pivot straight into a full investigation, and if the pattern is worth catching automatically going forward, it can become a new scheduled analytics rule. That loop from manual hunt to automated rule is the continuous-improvement practice from the maturity model, in action. Next up: bookmarks, for saving that evidence as a case builds.
